svg.title: P026. From sale lines to one row per category. Why each SQL step is necessary.
svg.desc: Follow the same sample through eight decisions. The left join keeps the four units of missing product 999. The full outer join adds unsold Stationery. The grouping keys separate sales with missing lookups. Two Drinks lines in order 100 yield one order, three units and 28 at list price. The final five category rows account for all eleven units. Blue, green and red bands identify the three source tables.
svg.text: From sale lines to one row per category
Find how many orders included each category, how many units sold, and their value at list price.
5 sale lines → 5 after the product lookup → 6 when Stationery joins → 5 category totals

g.aria-label: Step 1. Why start with OrderDetails?
g.text: One row is one sale line. Its quantity is what Finance needs to trace, even when a product or category lookup fails.

g.aria-label: 5 order lines
4 catalogue products
3 categories

g.text: Line 1 records two units of product 10. Product 10 points to category 1, Drinks.

g.aria-label: Step 2. Why LEFT JOIN to Products?
g.text: Products comes second to supply price and CategoryID. A LEFT JOIN keeps every sale line, including the four units on line 5.

g.aria-label: 5 sale lines → 5 joined rows · 4 sale-line columns + 3 product columns
g.text: 5 sale lines → 5 joined rows · 4 sale-line columns + 3 product columns
Line 5 bought four units of product 999. The blue 999 survives and the green product ID is NULL. The four units still count.

g.aria-label: Step 3. Why FULL OUTER JOIN to Category?
g.text: Why FULL OUTER JOIN to Category?
Use the CategoryID from Products to match Category third. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched sales and unsold categories such as Stationery.

g.aria-label: 5 joined rows → 6 rows · 7 previous columns + 2 category columns
g.text: 5 joined rows → 6 rows · 7 previous columns + 2 category columns
Line 4 survives with category 99 missing from the catalogue. Stationery enters from the other side as the sixth row.

g.aria-label: Step 4. Why label missing matches before grouping?
g.text: Why label missing matches before grouping?
A missing category can have two causes. Check which lookup succeeded so each sale goes into the right group.

g.aria-label: 6 rows → 6 labeled rows · add category_name

g.text: Line 4 found product 30 → Unmapped. Line 5 has no matching product → Unknown product. Stationery keeps its catalogue name.

g.aria-label: Step 5. Why multiply price by quantity on each line?
g.text: Why multiply price by quantity on each line?
Products can have different prices within one order. Each price belongs with the quantity on that same sale line.

g.aria-label: 6 labeled rows → 6 rows with a line value
g.text: 6 labeled rows → 6 rows with a line value
Both Drinks lines belong to order 100. They contribute 10 × 2 = 20 and 8 × 1 = 8.

g.aria-label: Step 6. Why group by the category ID and its label?
g.text: Why group by the category ID and its label?
The report needs one row per category. The ID keeps categories with the same name separate. The label separates groups with a missing ID.

g.aria-label: 6 working rows · the two grouping columns are underlined
g.text: 6 working rows · the two grouping columns are underlined

g.aria-label: 6 joined rows → 5 groups · which sale lines belong together?
g.text: 6 joined rows → 5 groups · which sale lines belong together?
Lines 1 and 2 share (1, Drinks). Lines 4 and 5 both have a NULL category ID, but their labels put them in separate groups.

g.aria-label: Step 7. Why count orders once but add every unit?
g.text: Why count orders once but add every unit?
One order can contain several sale lines in a category. Count distinct order IDs, add every quantity, and add the value of each priced line.

g.aria-label: Drinks · the two input rows used for the calculations below
g.text: Drinks · the two input rows used for the calculations below
Follow the two Drinks lines into the totals
A repeated order ID counts once.
Every unit from both lines counts.
A missing line ID means no sale.
Each line uses its own price.

g.aria-label: 5 groups → 5 totals · one row per category
g.text: 5 groups → 5 totals · one row per category
Stationery has zero real sale lines, so its value is 0. Unknown product has one sale of four units with no price, so its value is NULL.

g.aria-label: Step 8. Why sort by value and check the units?
g.text: Why sort by value and check the units?
The team allocates its promotion budget using category value. Rank known values highest first, then check the unit total against the original sale lines.
descending, NULL last. Break ties by

g.aria-label: 5 groups → 5 ranked rows · one row per category
g.text: 5 groups → 5 ranked rows · one row per category
Drinks leads at 28. A known zero for Stationery comes before the unknown value. If values tie, category name breaks the tie A–Z.
